transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. 

Um... I guess I'm here because I just feel like I don't deserve the trust people put in me right now. I'm a physician myself, and lately, I just keep replaying these small clinical imperfections in my head. Little things, really. But I can't stop going over them, and it just feels like they prove I'm a dangerous doctor. I just can't seem to shake that feeling, so I figured I needed to talk to someone.

When you find yourself replaying these clinical imperfections, do you feel an internal pressure or a need to perform any specific mental or physical actions to 'undo' the mistake or make yourself feel safe again?

No, not really. I don't do anything to try and undo it. Um... there's no specific action or mental trick I feel like I have to do. 

It's more just... the thoughts are just there, and they're heavy. I just kind of sit with the guilt and the feeling that I'm putting people at risk. I don't try to fix it in my head or do anything to make myself feel safe, I just... I just feel awful about it.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your sleep patterns or your appetite since these feelings began?

No, not really. Um... my sleep has been about the same as usual, I think. And my appetite hasn't really changed either. I'm still eating normally. So, no, I haven't noticed any significant changes in those areas.
When you are caught in these repetitive, heavy thoughts, do you ever feel as though you are detached from your own body or as if the world around you is somehow unreal or dreamlike?

No, I don't think so. I haven't felt like I'm outside my body or anything like that. And the world doesn't seem fake or like a dream. It all feels very real... just, you know, very heavy. But I'm definitely still here, in my own body, experiencing it.

Outside of these specific thoughts about your clinical work, do you find that you spend a large portion of your day worrying about other general aspects of your life, such as your finances, your personal relationships, or your health?

No, not really. I don't really worry much about that other stuff. My finances are fine, my health is okay, and things with my friends and family are pretty normal. It's really just the work stuff... the clinical things that I can't stop thinking about. The rest of my life isn't really on my mind like that.
Do these repetitive thoughts about your clinical work feel like they are coming from your own mind, or do they feel forced upon you against your will?

No, they definitely feel like they're my own thoughts. I mean, they're just my own worries about the patients and the decisions I've made. Nobody is putting them in my head or forcing them on me. It's just my own mind getting stuck on all the clinical details.
Did these persistent thoughts about your clinical work begin shortly after a specific, identifiable event or change in your professional life?
Yeah, it actually did. It started right after I received a clinic award. That was about... a year and a month ago. So, this has been going on for just over a year now, ever since I got that award.
Since this started after receiving that award, have you felt that this level of worry about your work performance has been present for most days during the past year?

Yeah, it really has. I'd say most days, definitely. Since that award, it's just been a constant thing... almost every day I'm caught up in these thoughts about my clinical decisions. It hasn't really let up.
Have these persistent thoughts about your clinical work interfered with your ability to perform your job or interact with your colleagues in the way you would like?

Yeah, it has. I mean, I’m still showing up to clinic, but... I’ve had to ask for help with a lot of the non-urgent administrative work. I just can't seem to get through it. And I pretty much avoid any social plans now. I just don’t trust my own judgment right now, and I really don't have the energy for it anyway. So it’s definitely started to affect how reliably I function at work, and... just how connected I am to people outside of it.
Do you find that you have lost interest or pleasure in the activities that you used to enjoy?

Yeah, I really have. I used to do a lot outside of work... planning weekend hikes, going out to take sunrise photos, cooking these big Indonesian dinners for my friends. But for months now, I just haven't wanted to do any of it. All of those things just feel like obligations now, and I really can’t make myself care about them anymore.
Have you noticed that your movements or the speed at which you speak or think have slowed down, or conversely, that you feel restless and unable to sit still?

Yeah, I've definitely slowed down. It's... it's mostly that everything just takes longer. At work, I move so slowly between patient rooms. And when I sit down to do my charts, I just end up staring at the electronic health record for a long time before I even click anything. It's gotten to the point where the nurses have started gently asking me if I'm okay because I'm just so... sluggish.
Looking back at your life before this past year, have you ever experienced a similar period of time where you felt this same level of low mood, loss of interest, and sluggishness?

No, I haven't. I mean... medical school and residency were definitely exhausting, and I had days where I was just burned out or tired, but... it was never like this. I've never had a period where I felt this consistently down or just completely lost interest in everything. This past year is really the first time I've ever experienced anything like this.
